title: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI
excerpt: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI. By PYMNTS | November 11, 2026. |. Banks are handing more work to artificial intelligence. Some AI tools now handle business activities like credit decisioning, customer service and fraud detection. That raises a simple question: Who makes sure these systems get it right? The nation’s top bank regulator offered its answer. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released Nov. 4 the “ OCC Supervisory Framework on Bank Use of Super Intelligence ,” a new guide to help its examiners review how banks use AI. The guide focuses on generative AI, which creates text and other content. It also covers agentic AI, which can take actions without a person stepping in each time. The OCC called this technology super intelligence , the term used by the executive branch in place of artificial intelligence, according to a Sept. 29 executive order signed by President Donald Trump. The guide doesn’t create new rules for banks , according to an analysis from law firm Ballard Spahr. It’s a resource for the people who inspect them. Banks won’t have to treat AI as its own risk category. Examiners will instead look at how AI changes the risks banks already manage. These include fraud, privacy, cybersecurity and work with outside vendors. The OCC built the guide around six areas, per the analysis. Examiners will ask what an AI system is allowed to do and what happens if it makes a mistake. They’ll look at the guardrails a bank has in place and who’s keeping watch. They’ll check how a bank recovers when a system fails. And they’ll want proof that the bank’s safety checks keep working over time. The guide also said risk depends on how much freedom an AI system has, according to the analysis. A simple bot that can start payments may pose more danger than a powerful model that only helps staff draft memos. To sort this out, the OCC laid out four risk levels. Payment bots that act on their own and instant credit decisions sit at the top. Internal tools that never touch customer data sit at the bottom. “[T]he more consequential and autonomous the activity, the more extensive the controls should be,” the analysis said. Human review gets a close look, too. The OCC warned that a person who just clicks “approve” doesn’t count as real oversight. Reviewers need the skills, the facts and the power to reject or stop what the AI is doing, per the analysis. Customers are a big focus. AI chatbots can give wrong answers about fees, interest rates or account balances. The OCC said these errors could lead to legal trouble and harm customers, according to the analysis. Banks can’t blame the machine, either. A bank is still on the hook if its AI breaks the law. Many banks buy their AI from outside companies, so vendors face extra scrutiny, the analysis said. The guide asked whether contracts spell out who pays when an AI tool causes harm. It also asked whether vendors must warn banks before they change how their AI works. A vendor could add new AI features to an old product, and the bank might not notice the new risks. So, what comes next? In a bulletin released with the guide, the OCC said the document sets no binding standards. Banks aren’t even expected to use it to grade their own AI programs. Still, the analysis said banks shouldn’t ignore it. The guide offers a clear preview of what examiners may ask about during future bank exams. Banks should study it closely and check whether their current risk and compliance programs already cover the issues the OCC raised. Banks that find gaps now may have an easier time when examiners come calling. For all PYMNTS AI coverage, subscribe to the daily AI newsletter. Recommended. title: Nigeria's Rex Africa Launches AI-Native Bank
excerpt: African Capital Markets. Invest in Africa New. English. Nigeria's Rex Africa Launches AI-Native Bank. STARTUP VENTURE CAPITAL November 11, 2026 at 11:59 AM UTC. TLDR. Nigerian fintech Rex Africa launched the country's first AI-native bank this month. The bank features Rex Atlas, an AI agent offering personalized financial guidance. Rex Africa built its own AI-integrated banking infrastructure, RexCore. Nigerian fintech startup Rex Africa has launched what it describes as the country’s first AI-native bank. The new banking service, which went live this month, is built around an AI-powered financial agent designed to provide customers with personalized guidance. Founded by Yinka Odeleye, Rex Africa aims to integrate artificial intelligence directly into the core banking experience. Central to its offering is Rex Atlas, an AI agent that analyzes users' financial history and allows conversational interaction. This agent delivers tailored recommendations on savings, investments, credit, and risk management. Chief Technology Officer Opeyemi Emmanuel emphasized that AI is fundamental to the banking experience, not merely an add-on feature. The platform provides a comprehensive suite of products for both individuals and businesses. Consumers can access flexible savings through RexSave, fixed-term savings via RexVault, and credit options with RexFlex, alongside payments using RexCard. For businesses, RexPOS enables payment acceptance, while RexCredit offers financing solutions for small and medium-sized enterprises and larger corporations. Since its launch this month, Rex has already onboarded thousands of individual users and hundreds of businesses. Rex operates under the license of Rex Microfinance Bank, which is regulated by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). Deposits made with the bank are eligible for insurance coverage by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC, providing a layer of security for users. He added that banking should evolve beyond transactional services to actively assist customers in managing, protecting, and growing their wealth. The company’s broader ecosystem extends beyond its consumer application. It includes an established lending business that has been operational for some time. Additionally, Rex maintains a live banking-as-a-service (BaaS) portal, which supports various functions such as customer accounts, collections, and payouts for other entities. Nigeria currently represents the immediate and primary market focus for Rex Africa. Key Takeaways. Rex Africa's launch of an AI-native bank in Nigeria represents a significant evolution in the country's fintech sector, moving beyond conventional digital banking to offer a deeply personalized financial experience. The company's strategic decision to embed artificial intelligence directly into its proprietary RexCore infrastructure from the outset, rather than adding it as a supplementary feature, reflects a core conviction that intelligence will fundamentally redefine the future of banking. This foundational integration enables the development of Rex Atlas, an AI-powered financial agent designed to analyze individual financial histories and facilitate conversational interactions. title: Kakao Pay Securities Builds AI-Based Fraud Detection System
excerpt: Kakao Pay Securities Builds AI-Based Fraud Detection System. by Kim Youngwon. Published 12 Nov. 2026 10:16(KST). Share Language Text Size Print. Machine Learning-Based Detection of Suspicious Activity Analyzes Access Environments and Fund Flows Strengthens Anti-Money Laundering Efforts with Expert Hire. Kakao Pay Securities said on November 12 that it has built an artificial intelligence-based fraud detection system (AI FDS) and has been using it in live transactions since this month. AI FDS combines the existing fraud detection framework with machine learning-based risk analysis. By learning from a wide range of transaction data and financial fraud cases, it identifies suspicious signs more precisely. It also detects connections between transactions and complex risk signals that may be difficult to identify from individual data points alone, and provides staff with the risk level of detected transactions and the basis for its assessment. Staff can then promptly review suspicious transactions and take necessary action. View original image. The system’s scope of detection has been expanded to reflect the nature of securities transactions, which involve cash, stocks, and foreign currencies. It covers not only deposits and withdrawals and account opening, but also stock sales, currency exchanges, transfers of stocks into and out of accounts held at other securities firms, and changes to user information. The aim is to combat financial fraud targeting securities accounts, such as cases in which criminals hijack an account, sell the stocks held in it, and withdraw the proceeds or transfer the stocks to another securities firm. The system also analyzes the environment in which transactions take place and the flow of funds. It combines various signals from transaction and access environments to identify situations in which account hijacking is suspected, while detecting signs of abnormal fund flows based on deposit and withdrawal patterns and connections between transactions. This is intended to address the risk of accounts being used for voice phishing, investment scams, illegal gambling, or illegal private lending. The company has also strengthened its organization and added specialized personnel so it can assess the money laundering risks associated with transactions suspected of involving financial fraud. In March 2026, it reorganized its structure to integrate the operation of fraud detection and anti-money laundering functions. In July 2026, it appointed an expert in anti-money laundering and financial consumer protection with 26 years of experience in the financial sector to lead the team. The company will also strengthen collaboration with its customer service center. It plans to improve the relevant systems so that, when suspicious transactions are detected, every step—from user verification and guidance to counseling, protective measures, and responses to customer losses—can be coordinated seamlessly. title: Agentic AI and financial crime: How banks can stay ahead
excerpt: Tieto Banktech. Without adequate protection from financial crime, agentic could stall. As consumers become more comfortable with agents and the number of agent-to-agent interactions soars, Øystein Namtvedt, Head of Engineering in Tieto Banktech’s Financial Crime Prevention team, considers how to protect agents from financial crime. Financial crime prevention solutions. Øystein Namtvedt 11 November 2026 3 min read. Consumers are becoming more comfortable with the idea of using agents for online shopping. While this is good news, steps must be taken to prevent fraudsters doing serious damage. Failure to do so could see the agentic economy stall – or worse. Table of contents. Agentic: already here for fraudsters, too. Banks and fintechs should understand the present reality of the agentic economy. Too often, we’re given the impression agents belong to the future. In fact, the number of agents in use across Europe is growing exponentially, as is agent-to-agent dialogue: in the last six months, the use of agents by European SMEs grew by more than 800%, according to Eurostat. Meanwhile, consumers no longer see agents as science fiction, with more than 50% of European consumers now saying they are comfortable using them to compare prices and find deals. At Tieto Banktech, our Defence Center constantly monitors global fraud trends to protect our clients and their end customers. Our analysis shows criminal groups are becoming more sophisticated, employing powerful new technologies to improve and scale their activities. For instance, social manipulation fraud grew by more than a third last year, as criminals successfully faked identities to dupe authentication mechanisms. Fighting this level of criminal sophistication needs a change of approach. Fraud teams should fight fire with fire, employing agentic AI to prevent new forms of ID theft, fraud and money laundering. And with new regulations ahead, using sophisticated machine learning techniques is likely the only way to stop fraud while keeping costs down. According to LexisNexis, every dollar lost to fraud this year (2026) will cost financial services firms $5. 47 in overheads, 52% of which is operational overheads and 48% the cost of reimbursement; a separate study by The American Bankers Association4 tell us these costs have more than doubled in the last two years. New regulations need new approaches. The EU’s new AML-R regulation will apply more stringent criteria in many categories from 2027, widening the scope of AML checks to include new merchant categories and new transaction types. Taking these new requirements into account alongside rapid growth in the sophistication of criminal techniques, it’s clear that using adaptive, self-regulating agentic models is the only way to combat criminal activity in the agentic age. Failure to do so creates two risks: firstly, the risk of repeated fraud by malicious agents that successfully overcome authentication systems; and secondly, an unsustainable increase in the cost and time banks devote to identifying fraud and money laundering. Fighting financial crime and maintaining regulatory compliance already costs Europe’s banks tens of billions every year. As the agentic economy grows, continuing to use existing approaches will place an unmanageable burden on banks unless they use agents and AI to fight fraud. To help banks in this fight, we’ve developed a modernized AML solution, AML Explore, which uses our proprietary ATLAS AI model, a self-supervised Large Financial Model, to detect emerging fraud vectors and suspicious transactions while reducing the number of false positives banks must review manually. Our internal data shows that this approach reduces false positives by 71%, saving huge amounts of time on false alerts, one of the biggest cost factors in AML defence. Taken together, these two products deliver a low-cost, highly effective fraud defence system that’s already in use by our core customers in the Nordics and elsewhere. Øystein

title: Sovereign AI and British Business Bank invest in British firm developing the next generation of AI hardware
excerpt: Press release Sovereign AI and British Business Bank invest in British firm developing the next generation of AI hardware. UK Government’s Sovereign AI and the British Business Bank back Fractile - a Bristol and London based frontier AI hardware firm developing advanced chips. From: Cabinet Office , Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade and British Business Bank Published: 11 November 2026. UK Government’s Sovereign AI and the British Business Bank back Fractile - a Bristol and London based frontier AI hardware firm developing advanced chips, as part of a funding round worth more than £500 million. Investment supports the government’s ambition to make Britain a world leader in developing the technology that powers artificial intelligence. Backing British companies will strengthen sovereign capabilities, reduce reliance on overseas technology and support highly skilled jobs and industrial renewal across the country. Fractile, a startup based across London and Bristol developing advanced chips - the physical hardware that powers artificial intelligence - has secured backing from the UK Government’s Sovereign AI Venture Fund and the British Business Bank as part of a round worth over £500 million. The investment, announced today [Wednesday 11 November], is another step in the government’s ambition to make Britain a world leader in the technologies that will shape the future of AI, ensuring that British scientific excellence translates into British companies, highly skilled jobs and industrial strength. It will also help strengthen Britain’s sovereign capabilities in critical technologies, reducing dependence on fragile overseas supply chains and ensuring the UK has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy. Fractile is re-inventing the hardware that AI runs on, so that it is faster, more energy efficient, and less costly. It is taking a unique approach, looking at the full stack of technologies that AI rests upon: from chips, to software and fundamental research into machine learning (the mathematical algorithms that underpin AI). Today’s funding round values the company at over £5 billion. Besides Sovereign AI and the British Business Bank, it is also being backed through this Series C round by investors including CapitalG, Lightspeed and Redpoint. From Alan Turing’s pioneering work to the creation of Arm in Cambridge, Britain has a proud history of laying the foundations for modern computing. Yet too often, the industrial and commercial rewards of British breakthroughs have been realised elsewhere. The government is determined to change that, backing ambitious homegrown companies to grow into global technology leaders while keeping more of the jobs, expertise and economic value they create here in Britain. Through Sovereign AI, the government is backing British chip designers, advanced hardware companies and AI entrepreneurs. By anchoring these critical capabilities on home soil, the government is safeguarding the UK’s critical infrastructure, keeping British data secure and ensuring the economic returns of technological breakthroughs directly benefit British workers. The British Business Bank is the UK’s economic development bank, helping innovative businesses access the finance they need to start up, scale up and stay in the UK. Their support will help the company access the long-term capital needed to scale its breakthrough AI hardware technology in the UK. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said:. For too long, Britain has produced some of the world’s best scientific ideas, only to see too much of the technology, industry and wealth they create built elsewhere. We are determined to change that. If AI is going to serve the British people, strengthen our public services and create good jobs across the country, Britain needs to build more of the technology that powers it. title: Northern Trust leans on Microsoft FDEs to boost agentic buildout
summary: The financial services firm cut analyst’s data preparation time by 83% with the use of an onboarding agent, the companies said.
excerpt: An article from. Dive Brief. Northern Trust leans on Microsoft engineers to boost agentic buildout. The financial services firm cut analyst data preparation time by 83% with the use of an onboarding agent, the companies said. Published Nov. 11, 2026. Makenzie Holland Senior News Writer. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. First published on. Dive Brief:. N orthern Trust worked with Microsoft Frontier Company’s forward-deployed engineering teams to build an artificial intelligence-powered onboarding agent that cuts data preparation time by 83% — from 2½ weeks to three days — for the financial services firm’s analysts, according to a Monday announcement. The agent consolidates customer data from multiple, disparate sources into a standardized format to ease new client onboarding. The agent is built on Microsoft Azure, using Microsoft Foundry for enterprise AI, and connects to Microsoft 365 tools. The foundation lets Northern Trust analysts review and approve the agent’s work while a governed intelligence layer preserves onboarding knowledge, letting the agent build expertise over time, the announcement said. The agent speeds the onboarding process for clients while maintaining oversight and controls, Pete Cherecwich, Northern Trust’s chief operating officer, said in the announcement. Dive Insight:. Northern Trust expanded its longstanding partnership with Microsoft to build the client onboarding agent, a move that comes as financial services firms navigate deploying advanced AI while maintaining security, privacy and governance controls. Accelerated AI use is prompting a heightened focus on governance and responsible AI use among financial institutions, according to an Evident report published last month. More than two-thirds of global financial firms surveyed by Evident for the report said they have added controls for AI systems. Northern Trust’s client onboarding agent combines “advanced AI with enterprise-grade privacy, security and governance to make the process faster for clients, ” Northern Trust CEO Michael O’Grady said last month during the financial services firm’s third-quarter earnings call. Human oversight has been embedded throughout the agent’s workflow, letting analysts evaluate the tool’s reasoning and review outputs, according to the Monday announcement. “This approach points to a broader opportunity across regulated industries to transform complex workflows and deliver business value without compromising trust,” Bill Borden, corporate vice president of worldwide financial services at Microsoft , said in the announcement. Alongside its client onboarding agent, Northern Trust has adopted client action plan agents, which O’Grady said save customer relationship managers two to three hours per client memo. AI-enabled digitization has also nearly doubled straight-through processing, or automated financial transactions, for the company. Internally, the bank’s AI assistant Byron supports wealth managers with more tailored insights to deliver to clients, he added. AI deployment and use of its proprietary platform has helped deliver efficiency and productivity gains to the bank, O’Grady t old shareholders in a 2025 report. “Our approach is disciplined, starting with outcomes, simplifying processes and redesigning work rather than just adding tools,” O’Grady said during the earnings call. title: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says
excerpt: . Richard Adams Education editor. Updated Wed, 11 November 2026 at 10:57 am UTC. 2. Universities should go back to traditional exams and in-person presentations to grade students after lecturers complained that AI has made it “close to impossible” to assess coursework, according to an investigation by England’s higher education regulator. The Office for Students (OfS) said the credibility of degrees from England’s universities was under threat from the prolific use of AI in essays, dissertations and “open book” exams, with students reporting that their peers boasted of using AI undetected by staff. The regulator warned universities and other higher education institutions that failing to design “valid and reliable measures of students’ knowledge and skills” to combat AI could breach their conditions of registration and lead to sanctions being imposed. Related: AI may be denting computer science graduates’ job prospects, UK data shows. Josh Fleming, the director of strategy and delivery at the OfS, said AI use in higher education “presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students’ learning and institutions’ ability to assess them”. Fleming added: “We need to see far greater efforts to tackle these risks, including far greater use of AI-free assessment. “The scale and pace of both the challenge and opportunity presents a novel challenge for the sector and us as the regulator. We will continue to work with universities and colleges to help them reap the benefits of AI while avoiding the risks. ”. The OfS said many institutions had already redesigned how they assessed students to reduce potential AI misuse, including greater use of in-person written exams or oral examinations known as vivas. Other examples include students critiquing or editing AI-generated output, or “process-based” assessments where students detail how they researched and produced their work. A Department for Education spokesperson said: “We expect universities to take this issue seriously and we expect the OfS to both enforce the existing standards effectively, and work at pace to ensure its regulatory framework is explicit, strong and durable on the use of AI. ”. A spokesperson for Universities UK , which represents 147 higher education institutions, said: “There is further to go but many have made substantial changes to how they assess students. This includes more in-person exams, presentations, vivas, process-based assessment and assessments that integrate AI in a controlled way. ”. The report by the OfS and Advance HE , a charity promoting university governance and teaching, interviewed more than 300 students and staff at 127 universities and colleges this year, to gauge AI policies and use in teaching and assessment. One academic told the researchers: “AI has put academic integrity at serious risk … coursework is now overwhelmingly written in part, or exclusively, with the help of AI. ”. Related: Smartglasses and earpieces may worsen exam cheating in schools, says Ofqual. Another university staff member said: “I think we’re realising that a number of our assessments may be unfit for purpose, and that pervasive use of AI may render our assessment of students close to impossible in some areas. ”. The survey found that AI use was rife, with students saying their colleagues completed assessments using AI “sometimes in just a few minutes” and received similar grades to those who had completed an assessment without AI. “Some students described their peers being unable to recall basic details about the assessment they had just submitted,” the report noted. One student told the researchers: “I’ve had people admit, peer to peer, ‘I wrote this whole essay with ChatGPT’ … then they don’t get caught, they get a good grade probably, and then because it worked the first time, they do it on their next assessment. ”. Academics also described receiving large numbers of submissions that looked the same, referenced the same literature

Big bank boss warns AI job cuts could spark a global crisis
excerpt: Nuno Matos has told parliament that AI-driven job losses could trigger a worldwide crisis and that it should be regulated. By Matthew Sellers. 12 Nov 2026. Share. ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos has warned that artificial intelligence could set off an international jobs crisis, and says the world needs global rules to stop it. If AI led to job cuts of up to 50 per cent, “it’s going to be a global crisis”, Matos told a parliamentary hearing in Canberra on Thursday. He described AI as one of the few areas where he believed global regulation was needed. His advice for workers in the meantime was more down to earth. Those who build AI skills lower their risk of losing out to more proficient colleagues, he said, pointing to ANZ’s work developing staff capability in-house. For HR leaders, that is the part of his evidence that lands closest to home, because most Australians using AI at work are teaching themselves. What Matos told the committee. ANZ was the first of the big four banks to appear before the House of Representatives economics committee this week. Asked about AI by independent MP Allegra Spender, Matos said he couldn’t say whether the technology would have a net positive, net negative, or neutral impact on jobs in Australia or globally. He added that anything he said now could be wrong in six months, given how quickly AI is moving. He told the committee that none of ANZ’s recent job cuts were caused by AI, but he couldn’t guarantee there would be no AI-related job losses in future. Almost 3,500 ANZ employees left in the year to September, the bank reported on Monday. Over the same period, its statutory net profit rose 23 per cent to $7. 27 billion. Matos also said wide adoption of AI without proper guardrails was a serious problem, and that no bank should build AI without the right controls. ANZ is developing its own control platform as it rolls the technology out across the bank. Offshoring also came up. Of ANZ’s 40,000 employees, about 18,000 are in Australia and 7,000 in New Zealand, with up to 9,000 in India and the Philippines, AAP reported. Matos said offshoring had been standard practice for decades, and that ANZ’s offshore headcount had actually fallen by 600 in 2026. Read next: CBA reverses AI-triggered employee layoffs. Regulation is coming, but not for most employers. Matos’s call for global rules came days after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese unveiled a plan to legislate safety and security obligations for frontier AI companies operating in Australia, enforced by a new AI safety regulator. Employment lawyers told HRD that most employers are unlikely to be directly covered , because the rules target the companies that build advanced AI models rather than the businesses that use them. The lawyers still saw a clear signal for HR in the proposal. Dentons partner Paul O’Halloran said organisations should map where AI is used across the business and who is accountable when something goes wrong. In his words, “employers should not wait for the legislation”. The training gap. Matos’s advice assumes workers can get the skills he’s describing. The local data suggests many are doing it without help. Hays : In its FY26/27 Salary Guide survey of more than 6,500 professionals, Hays found 78 per cent of Australians using AI at work had no formal training. Forty-two per cent said upskilling wasn’t formally supported in their organisation, or they didn’t know what options were available. Dayforce: In research HRD reported in October last year, 81 per cent of employees believed employers should reskill workers affected by AI , but only 17 per cent of organisations were doing so. Employment Hero : A survey by the HR software company found about a third of Australian workers use AI tools at work without their employer knowing. That last figure matters for Matos’s own argument. Tamilnad Mercantile Bank Launches AI Services, New Branch
excerpt: Home Breaking News Tamilnad Mercantile Bank Launches AI Services, New Branch. Breaking News. Tamilnad Mercantile Bank Launches AI Services, New Branch. By Ayesha Siddiqui. November 12, 2026. 0. Copy URL. Facebook. Linkedin. X. WhatsApp. Tamilnad Mercantile Bank has launched a multilingual AI telecalling service, a Smart Kiosk, a new credit card and a branch in Thoothukudi as it marked its 105th Foundation Day, combining technology-led customer services with an expansion of its physical banking network. The initiatives were unveiled at celebrations in Thoothukudi, where Vice-President of India C P Radhakrishnan called on the bank to strengthen its national presence and aspire to become one of India’s leading private sector banks. The event was attended by Tamil Nadu Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar, TMB’s part-time chairman K Ramachandran, executive director Vincent Menachery, board members and senior bank officials. TMB managing director and chief executive officer Salee S Nair said the bank would focus on becoming more agile, technology-driven and customer-centric. The bank’s new TMB Vani service is an AI-powered telecalling platform designed to communicate with customers in 40 languages, while the Smart Kiosk is intended to expand technology-enabled customer interactions. The bank also introduced an auto-reconciliation solution to improve operational efficiency and launched a new credit card. A branch was inaugurated virtually in Anna Nagar, Thoothukudi, extending TMB’s physical banking presence in its home city. Radhakrishnan traced the bank’s history from its origin as Nadar Bank Ltd in 1921 to its current network of 632 branches across 17 states and four Union Territories. The bank serves more than 53 lakh customers and has total business exceeding ₹1. 30 trillion, according to details cited at the event. The Vice-President highlighted the role of banks in supporting micro, small and medium enterprises, farmers, entrepreneurs and women-led enterprises. He also linked digital initiatives such as UPI to broader financial inclusion and the national development objective of Viksit Bharat @2047. Radhakrishnan urged TMB to maintain strong cybersecurity systems as it expands its digital services, specifically emphasising the need to protect customers’ money and personal data. He also asked the bank to remain rooted in Thoothukudi while pursuing a wider national footprint. Alongside the customer-facing services, TMB announced a careers portal for prospective job seekers and the LinkedIn Learning Platform, an employee learning and development initiative. Nair said the technology and workforce initiatives would support the bank’s effort to strengthen capabilities and expand its reach. The bank’s next phase will involve implementing the newly announced services and products across its operating network while continuing to combine its legacy branch presence with digital banking tools, according to statements made during the Foundation Day programme. Nigeria’s Rex Africa launches AI-native bank with conversational financial agent
excerpt: Nigerian fintech startup Rex Africa has launched what it says is the country’s first AI-native bank, built around an AI-powered financial agent that gives customers personalised guidance on saving, investing and borrowing. Founded by Yinka Odeleye, Rex Africa has built its own banking infrastructure, RexCore, with AI integrated from the outset rather than added on later. At the heart of the offering is Rex Atlas, an agent that analyses users’ financial history and lets them interact with their bank conversationally, offering tailored recommendations on savings, investments, credit and risk management. “We built Rex with AI at the heart of the banking experience, not as an additional feature,” said chief technology officer Opeyemi Emmanuel. Alongside the agent, Rex offers a suite of products for individuals and businesses. Consumers can access flexible savings through RexSave, fixed-term savings via RexVault, credit through RexFlex, and payments with RexCard. For businesses, RexPOS enables payment acceptance, while RexCredit provides SME and corporate financing. “Our founding conviction at Rex is that the next generation of banking will be defined by intelligence,” said Odeleye. “We believe banking should go beyond moving money to understanding customers and helping them manage, protect and grow their wealth. ”. Rex is powered by Rex Microfinance Bank, which is licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), with eligible deposits insured by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC). Beyond its consumer app, the company’s ecosystem includes an established lending business and a live banking-as-a-service (BaaS) portal that supports customer accounts, collections and payouts. Rex says it has already signed up thousands of individual users and hundreds of businesses since launching this month. Nigeria is the company’s immediate focus.

title: Students passing university assessments in minutes using AI, regulator warns
excerpt: . Hazel Shearing - Education correspondent. Updated Wed, 11 November 2026 at 8:01 am UTC. 0. Too many university students can use AI to complete assessments without staff finding out, the higher education regulator in England has said. The Office for Students (OfS) said "a significant proportion" of assessments are unsupervised and many can be completed to a high standard with AI, sometimes in minutes. It said this posed a "significant risk" to their credibility, and closed-book and practical exams were the most effective forms of assessments. Universities UK said many institutions had "made substantial changes" to make assessments "AI-proof". Universities that do not meet OfS quality standards could soon be banned from charging increased tuition fees or have caps imposed on their student numbers, under proposals that are now being consulted on. The new research from the OfS and Advance HE, a charity that gives awards for teaching excellence, is based on the views of 244 higher education staff and 91 students from at least 127 universities. It said "a significant proportion of assessments" were in "unsupervised, non-controlled formats where AI can be accessed by students completing them". "Many of these can be completed to a high standard using AI tools with limited engagement from students," it added. It also concluded it was "frequently possible" for students to use AI "in ways that cannot be reliably detected". Unsupervised assessment can include coursework, but also remote online exams. They were rolled out widely during Covid, and research from Swansea University last year suggests 93 universities in the UK still use them in some form. Josh Fleming, director of strategy and delivery at the OfS, said there were "fantastic" examples of universities seizing opportunities presented by AI, but there should be "far greater use of AI-free assessment". "It also presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students' learning and institutions' ability to assess them," he said. Advertisement. The research said AI literacy for students was important during and after university, and some institutions were clearly communicating to students where AI can and cannot be used in assessments. title: Forrester Expects 40% of Banks to Launch AI Assistants in 2027
excerpt: Forrester expects 40% of banks to launch AI assistants in 2027, as the firm forecasts a broader shift in banking that includes changes to operating models and consolidation of financial technology platforms. The firm’s Predictions 2027: Banking And Investing, dated Oct. 14, lists AI-native operating models, retail investment participation and platform consolidation among the forces expected to shape banking and investing. Principal Analyst Aurelie L’Hostis detailed three forecasts in an Oct. 22 post: bank launches of AI assistants, AI transformation programs and increased mergers and acquisitions in AI banking technology. Forrester says banks will need proprietary data, decisioning capabilities and specialist expertise to distinguish their AI assistants. The launch forecast concerns customer-facing tools, while the transformation forecast concerns broader changes to banks’ operations. The firm predicts one-third of banks will announce AI transformation programs and gives 5% as the success figure. Forrester also warns that some banks may relabel existing AI work without changing their operating models. Forrester expects mergers and acquisitions in AI banking technology to rise 50% in 2027. It says buyers will seek scale, proprietary data, governance and orchestration capabilities. The forecast places platform consolidation alongside banks’ efforts to build AI capabilities. L’Hostis said organizations that bring together data, decision systems and customer trust would be better positioned to support financial outcomes. “The winners will be the organizations that combine proprietary data, decisioning, orchestration, and trust to help customers achieve better financial outcomes. ”.
